demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Maladaptive Strategies.value: mentally rehearse worst case scenarios to feel prepared
Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively

issues.item: Triggers: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: These trigger items are not clinically coherent with the indexed trauma of unexpected/traumatic death of a loved one. Snake-related and pregnancy/birth reminders imply trauma contexts unrelated to bereavement, and there is no supporting threat or memory content linking them to this loss.

issues.item: Triggers: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: Avoiding military/police uniforms or weapons similarly implies a trauma context involving violence, combat, or armed threat, which is unsupported by the stated trauma type and by the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: For an index trauma of unexpected/traumatic death of a loved one, pregnancy/birth reminders are hard to justify unless the death specifically involved childbirth or infant loss; nothing else in the profile supports that context. This makes the trigger clinically implausible relative to the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons
issues.explanation: Avoiding military/police uniforms or weapons implies a trauma context involving combat, assault, or armed responders. That does not fit the rest of this bereavement-focused profile and is not supported by the other trigger, threat, or strategy items, so it appears incoherent with the trauma type and overall formulation.

vignette: Arjun had not expected anything to change on that Tuesday in October, but the phone call did. His younger brother, Vikram, had collapsed during a morning run and was gone before the paramedics could reach him. The suddenness of it left Arjun with no preparation, only the raw shock of a doorway closing without warning. When the first anniversary approached, Arjun deliberately left the firm’s studio at noon, telling clients his vehicle needed urgent attention, because the sight of that date on his phone made his chest tighten. He had come to believe that acknowledging the date was somehow inviting the same sudden loss, so he buried his calendar under blank weekends and double-booked site visits. His body braced for a second emergency. The silent alarm fired long before his mind could name the fear. The world kept offering grief, and Arjun kept turning away. When a longtime friend called to announce his mother had passed, Arjun listened for exactly forty seconds before excusing himself to a parking garage, his breath coming in shallow pulls. He was certain that listening to others mourn was a rehearsal for his own collapse, so he stopped attending community memorial services. He told colleagues he was pulled into tight renovation deadlines, though the truth was that walking past cemetery gates or sitting in a funeral parlor made his vision tunnel and his shoulders seize. What frightened him most was the way the scent of lilies or the sound of a hearse would drop him back into the hospital corridor waiting room. During a site inspection at a client’s mid-century renovation, a contractor’s radio crackled with a news bulletin about a sudden cardiac arrest. Arjun was suddenly on his knees, pressing his palms against the hardwood floor, acting as if he were back in that corridor. He stood abruptly, knocking over a level, and his frustration with the radio’s volume quickly spilled over into a sharp rebuke directed at the site foreman. His voice had carried that familiar, jagged edge that left him hollow afterward. Over the following months, he systematically declined projects involving estate clearances or grief-support spaces, rerouting those commissions to younger associates. He had started mentally cycling through worst-case scenarios when Priya stayed late at work, his mind constructing elaborate chains of hospital rooms, flatlining monitors, and empty hallways, just so he could feel ready. The mental loops never ended in resolution; they only ended when he forced himself to close his eyes and count to one hundred. He stopped inviting friends to his house after dusk because the quiet made the floorboards creak like footsteps in an empty wing, and he found himself snapping at Priya when she reached for his shoulder, his instinct to recoil outpacing his awareness of her warmth. The distance between them had grown not from any single argument, but from the quiet accumulation of canceled dinners, declined invitations to brotherly gatherings, and the careful choreography of rooms he never let himself inhabit. What finally brought Arjun to the clinic was the way his studio had begun to feel like a waiting room. He had realized he could no longer sketch a layout without checking the clock, could no longer sit through a zoning meeting without his fingers tracing the edge of the table as if bracing for impact. He did not want to live like a man constantly standing by a door that might open at any second. He was hoping to find a way to sit at his desk without his body turning against him, to look at a calendar without flinching, and to let a conversation about loss pass through him without closing the doors entirely. He wanted to stop rehearsing the future he was certain would break, and to simply sit in the present, even when it felt too quiet to trust.
